extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy writers (GOLD Comedy audience; women and nonbinary folks)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance on constructing short standup jokes by learning and applying the core joke structures (setup→punch, triples/lists, comparisons, character/act-out, callbacks, and tags). Emphasizes how to build jokes that land in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup…punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Set people up to expect one thing, then surprise them by going in a different and unexpected direction that, once heard, makes sense in a new way — that surprise is the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core structure for most jokes. Example: Henny Youngman — “Take my wife. Please.” (first phrase creates an expectation; second phrase reverses it). Use short, clear setups to create an expectation and a concise, surprising pivot for the punch. Examples also include Maysoon Zayid: “I’m not drunk. But the doctor who delivered me was.” Workshop examples: Emika: “I love to inspire people. I also love to see them fail.” Thea: “I am not just a nerd. I am also a geek.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple (rule of three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setup, setup, PUNCH — list three items where the third differs from the first two; the #3 must be different and provides the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common patterns: normal, normal, RANDOM; normal, normal, ALARMING (Jon Stewart example: Thanksgiving story ending with 'I killed them and took their land'); general, general, SUPER SPECIFIC; short, short, REALLY LONG. The third element doesn't have to be an earth-shattering twist — it simply must contrast with the first two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists
rubrics_metrics.description: A list joke has more than three elements (if three, it's a triple). Lists work by contrasting elements and can be hilarious through sheer length/accumulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous example: George Carlin’s '7 words you can’t say on TV.' Lists work best when elements contrast widely. They can be funny by being extremely long and are often about form and delivery (the faster, the better). Example from a workshop alum: a long, contrasting fear list: 'Wax Vacs, heights, loneliness, darkness, Russia, transphobia, homophobia, white supremacists, nails, and push pins.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons / Simile
rubrics_metrics.description: Using similes or comparisons to make a comedic point — 'X is like Y' — drawing humor from the incongruity of the comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic device from English class; can be used to highlight absurdity via unexpected analogies. Examples: Lynn Harris: 'That’s like beating the Italians at opera!' Tiffany Haddish: 'It looks like a Bedazzler threw up on it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Character / Act-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation-based joke where the performer shows rather than tells — doing a voice or physical behavior to create the character, rather than mere description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More about imitation than impersonation — avoid showy celebrity impressions (e.g., 'please don’t' do a DeNiro impression). Doing the voice/act makes the bit funnier than simply saying the trait. Advanced use: character can be used as commentary (e.g., Sasheer Zamata performing racist caricatures to critique them). The act does not need to be accurate; it needs to be funny and serve the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference to an earlier joke, line, or standout word later in the set; it rewards the audience for remembering and creates a feeling of inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callbacks themselves don't have to be inherently funny — their value is in recognition and payoff. They are effective for closing and reinforcing themes in a set. Example: reusing a standout word or earlier gag (the article cites 'YARDBIRDS!' as a payoff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag (5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short bonus joke appended to the end of an already complete joke; the original joke stands without it, but the tag usually gets an extra laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags do not need to be full jokes — they can be a repeated word, an underscored emotion ('Yup. Weird.' / 'YIKES'), or a small added detail that stretches the laugh (Brooke Van Poppelen example: adding 'International' to extend a joke about workout clothes). Tags provide a free extra laugh and can be used to build or prolong the payoff.
